sections.h2: What a hospital of around fifty beds should actually buy
paras: A fifty-bed hospital usually has an owner who is still a practising consultant, three or four people in the office who each do several jobs, a pharmacy, a small laboratory, mostly cash patients and a growing but modest amount of TPA work. It has no IT department and nobody who can spend a fortnight on configuration. The software question at this size is not which modules exist. It is which ones go live first and who has the hours to make that happen.

The honest answer is to run registration, the outpatient department, beds, pharmacy and billing from day one, because those five touch every rupee and every patient. Laboratory, imaging, procurement and the management dashboard follow once the first set is habit. HIMS is delivered to a fixed scope on a 30-working-day framework where scope allows, set up with your own data and taught at your own counters by the founder who built it, so the owner's clinical week is not the thing that pays for the rollout.

sections.h2: The hospital is big enough to need a system and too small to survive a bad one.
sections.lead: At this size a failed rollout is not a delay. It is six months back on the register.

items.h: The owner is the project team
items.p: Every decision about how the hospital should work comes back to the consultant, between clinics.
Vendors switch on all the modules on day one, the staff cannot cope, and the registers quietly come back.
The same person registers patients, raises the bill, runs the TPA file and orders the drugs.
The system has to be fast at the counter first and clever about claims second, not the other way round.
A machine in a back room becomes somebody's unpaid second job and then somebody's emergency.

sections.h2: Phases a fifty-bed hospital can actually absorb.

steps.p: A fixed list of what goes live first, written down before anything is configured.
Registration under UHID, outpatient consultation and e-prescription, beds, pharmacy and billing.
The front desk, the nursing station and the pharmacy counter are each taught their own screens.
Laboratory, TPA claims and inpatient running bills once phase one is routine.
Procurement, asset register, imaging through AuraPACS and the owner's dashboard.
Support on WhatsApp, with changes agreed as scope rather than raised as tickets.

sections.h2: Software for a 50 bed hospital, answered.

items.q: Do we have to switch everything on at once?
items.a: No, and you should not. Registration, outpatients, beds, pharmacy and billing go live first because they touch every patient and every payment. Laboratory, TPA and the dashboard follow once the first set is routine. It is the same records throughout, so nothing is migrated twice.

items.q: We have no IT staff. Who runs it?
items.a: Your existing desk, nursing and pharmacy staff run it, each on their own screens. HIMS is deployed in the cloud and used from a browser on the computers you already have, so there is no server for anyone to maintain.

items.q: How much of the owner's time does go-live need?
items.a: Decisions about rates, users and workflow need the owner. Configuration, data migration and training are done by the founder who built the software, in person in Chennai or remotely elsewhere in India.
There is no published price. Scope for a hospital this size is agreed on a call and quoted against that scope. See HIMS pricing for how the conversation works.

items.q: How is this different from software for a 100 bed hospital?
items.a: At fifty beds one desk usually does everything and the owner is still clinical. At a hundred there are shift handovers, a billing desk per area and an administrator who needs daily numbers. See software for a 100 bed hospital.
Modules are switched on against the same patient records rather than replaced. Adding a laboratory, imaging or a second branch is configuration, not a new implementation.
